stories.headline: How Brady Tkachuk (and the Senators) are preparing for his Ottawa return
stories.summary: After a summer blockbuster, the former Senators captain will be playing his first game against his old team (and its vocal fans).
stories.body:
It was a picture-perfect moment for Brady Tkachuk.

He was shoulder to shoulder with Florida Panthers general manager Bill Zito, having just concluded a news conference officially welcoming him to the organization following a trade days earlier from the Ottawa Senators. Tkachuk had pulled on his new No. 8 sweater and wore it with the satisfied grin of a cat who'd caught the canary. Of a man who had everything he asked for.

Because Tkachuk had. Asked for it, that is.

Rewind not two months before that introduction on June 23, and a very different media session was playing out with Tkachuk front and center as captain of the Senators. It was April 29, and Ottawa was four days removed from being swept by Carolina in its first-round Stanley Cup playoff series. Emotions were raw and rumors were rampant -- mainly surrounding Tkachuk.

Was his heart still with the organization that drafted him fourth overall in 2018 and signed him to a seven-year, $57.5 million contract extension in 2021 -- right before he accepted the Senators' captaincy and became the face of their franchise?

Tkachuk was insulted by the question.

"I feel like I've answered this hundreds of times," he said. "None of those things [about wanting to leave Ottawa] ever came out of my mouth. Quite honestly, it's just getting frustrating. It's becoming a distraction. I have been fully committed to this team, to this city, and it's just become a distraction and frustrating to deal with."

Tkachuk said his peace, but that mic drop was only for the cameras. Behind closed doors, he asked to be moved out of Canada's capital to join his brother, Matthew, and the two-time Stanley Cup-winning Panthers. That truth came from GM Steve Staios. He grappled with his star player asking to jump ship and then being limited in the trade process by a full no-movement clause attached to Tkachuk's contract.

There was only one place for which Tkachuk was willing to waive it. So, Staois delivered Tkachuk to the Sunshine State in a blockbuster deal June 21 that brought back a trio of first-round draft choices (two in 2026 and one in 2029) plus a 2027 second-round selection to the Senators.

When the deed was done, Staios declined to comment on Tkachuk's reasons for requesting a trade -- but the outcome was entirely driven by Tkachuk.

"He wanted to be traded," Staios said in June. "I was always fully supportive and wanted to make it work long term. I think it became clear as [last] season went on that maybe something was amiss."

Tkachuk explained himself eventually. The forward left town -- with 213 goals in 572 games -- on the wings of a social media post thanking the Ottawa fans and community for their support during his eight-year run. That sentiment fell flat in the gaping disconnect between his words and actions. Inevitably, Tkachuk would have to face the music -- in person -- and Florida's schedule had the reunion on fast-track, less than three weeks into Tkachuk's first season in new threads.

It will be no ordinary night Wednesday (7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN+), when the visiting Panthers will feel targeted in a whole different way by a fanbase riled up over Tkachuk's unceremonious departure in search of a "new chapter" he never admitted to wanting.

"There were definitely a lot of different things that happened throughout my time [in Ottawa]." Tkachuk said in the wake of the trade. "It wasn't an easy decision, it was something I took a little bit more time with than what's been [said] out there. It was a very hard decision. There's a lot more things that go into it, but for me now, just very thankful for what [the Senators] have done for me, not just as a player, but molding me into the human that I am today."

TKACHUK THE SEQUEL was a slow burn in Florida.

The first Tkachuk landing came when Matthew -- disgruntled in Calgary and unwilling to sign an extension there -- was traded to Florida in a July 2022 blockbuster. The chemistry clicked from Game 1, with Tkachuk scoring in his Panthers debut and tallying three goals and eight points through six games.

Brother Brady looked pedestrian by comparison, with zero goals and zero points for Florida heading into its seventh game of this season against Columbus.

The lack of production from Brady Tkachuk -- after willing his way onto the Panthers' roster -- led critics and comics alike to chime in on the stagnation. But then Tkachuk issued a rebuttal. In the second period against the Blue Jackets, he scored a natural hat trick to guide Florida to a 7-3 win (Matthew, of course, assisted on the trio of strikes).

Two nights later, Tkachuk was back punching in another natural hat trick in Florida's 3-2 overtime victory against Vancouver. That made him the first Panthers player to post consecutive natural hat tricks and only the third skater ever to do it.

He now had the necessary confidence boost ahead of what is sure to be a tumultuous homecoming in Ottawa.

"Today was pretty special," Tkachuk said. "It's pretty cool, but I know my goal in being here, and that's being part of something special, not just the individual stuff. It is great, but there are bigger goals out there."

Tkachuk notched the second of his momentous nights on home ice, prompting acknowledgement of the warm reception he'd enjoyed thus far.

"It's such an amazing fanbase, such amazing people here," Tkachuk said of Florida's faithful. "To feel the support from them, it meant a lot to me."

IT'S LIKELY THAT the greeting Tkachuk receives up north will be frostier. The Senators held a "Chuk Your Tkachuk" promotion in July when fans could trade in their former captain's sweater for a discount on other team merchandise. And even Ottawa's local baseball team, the Titans, hosted a "Forget Brady Day" that same month when fans could swap their Tkachuk jersey (when he still wore No. 7) for the No. 7 jersey of Titans infielder AJ Wright; 52 fans took them up on the offer.

The intermittent months of cooling off don't lessen the emotions. Tkachuk claims, at least, he's ready for anything when stepping back into the Senators' ring.

"I don't really have an expectation," Tkachuk said of the crowd reaction. "Whatever it is, it just shows how great of a fanbase it is. If it's negative, it just shows how passionate the fans are, and why I enjoyed playing in front of them. If it's positive, I'm just really grateful for my time there."

Tkachuk will make the best of what's thrown his way. He told Matthew on Tuesday's episode of their "Wingman" podcast that if any of his old No. 7 sweaters are disgruntledly tossed onto the ice during Wednesday's tilt, he will make sure they're donated to the Boys and Girls Club in Ottawa.

Clearly the reunion is on Tkachuk's mind to some degree, but his former teammates claim they're not giving it much thought.

"Brady's not really a topic of conversation in our dressing room," Nick Cousins said. "We don't really talk about it at all ... but I think it's going to be an emotional night for him."

True, because there is only one main character in this week's drama. And the anxiety over reaching a significant return game can -- like Tkachuk's ponderous start to his scoring career in Florida -- be unexpectedly delayed. It was for John Tavares.

Perhaps better than most, Tavares can appreciate and anticipate what awaits Tkachuk. Granted, Brady has Matthew to lean on when processing any emotions. But Matthew wasn't the Flames captain when he orchestrated an exit. Tavares was that for the New York Islanders when, in 2018, he passed on returning to the Islanders and left for Toronto in free agency.

Islanders fans were ruthless in attacking Tavares' decision -- the social media post of him in Leafs bedsheets as a child heralding the news of his eight-year contract didn't help matters there -- and Tavares had to eventually pay the piper in February 2019. The hostile crowd on Long Island didn't hold back, letting Tavares have it each time he touched the puck with boos and chants of "We Don't Need You" or "It's Your Bedtime," among other things.

Toronto played Edmonton at home the night before that reunion, and Tavares' focus had been trained fully on the Oilers. It wasn't until Tavares was cooling down postgame -- and was approached by former president of hockey operations Brendan Shanahan -- that the full weight of his next outing hit him.

"I remember Brendan coming up to talk to me, and just trying to help and be supportive," Tavares recalled. "And I think I realized then that going back would be something more than I was used to. I think I knew there'd be a lot of attention and noise about it, but I think it wasn't until then where, all at once, it really clicked that this was going to be something I hadn't experienced before, and there's going to be a lot of mixed emotions."

Tavares still speaks warmly about Islanders fans -- who continued taunting him during the Leafs' subsequent visits to Long Island -- and admits the support they offered during his nine-year stint was part of what made signing elsewhere so agonizing. It's much the same tone Tkachuk has tried to deliver, although he asked for the change and Tavares earned the right to make one.

Regardless, Tavares' tip is to be grateful. When the comeback inevitably feels heavy, hold on to the good memories.

"As difficult as the reception can be, if it's more on the negative side, I think just remind yourself to always acknowledge those feelings, too, because it's important," Tavares said. "Not everyone's privy to being inside your head or in your shoes, and living the ins and outs of your life, or really seeing or getting an understanding of what goes on, and what happens in terms of your career.

"Going back to a place you moved on from that meant a lot to you, and where you meant a lot to the organization and the fans, everyone's going to have their opinion. But just be appreciative of the way people believed in you. It is really meaningful if you ever get to have that."

Ottawa will have to manage its feelings, too. Coach Travis Green said his expectations over the fan response "doesn't matter at all," but it will be on Green to ensure his group isn't distracted by the extra energy.

"There will be a lot of emotion in the game and in the building. There always is when a player of that magnitude first comes back," Green said. "Whenever there's a game [like that], it's exciting. This will be a real fun game to play in. There's always some buildup the first time coming back ... but I'm not going to overthink it."

TKACHUK'S PUBLIC RATIONALE for abdicating his post in Ottawa has zeroed in on two factors: Florida's championship pedigree and the opportunity to suit up with Matthew in the NHL after successful international tournaments.

The brothers played together for Team USA at the 4 Nations Face-Off in February 2025 and then again at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. Winning gold there -- after a runner-up finish at 4 Nations -- was an unforgettable experience that made the comedown from Ottawa's quick playoff ouster seemingly more difficult to swallow. Tkachuk had already watched Matthew win two Stanley Cups with the Panthers before going through the high of securing gold with him overseas. He wanted it all, too.

Their dad, Keith -- an NHL legend and soon-to-be Hockey Hall of Fame inductee -- couldn't fault Brady for following his heart.

"They've dreamt of playing together," Keith Tkachuk said this summer. "They had an opportunity in the Olympics and [at] the 4 Nations. They're best friends, they wanted to do this together, and fortunately, it worked out. Both parties found a way to get it done."

Still, Brady told Matthew on a June episode of their podcast his true priority in selecting Florida for his second act.

"I made this decision taking you out of it. It wasn't about you," Brady said. "You know how much I love you, but every single time after playing you guys, I was like, 'Holy cow, that team is incredible and they have a chance to win every single year.'"

At least one of Tkachuk's friends in Ottawa and on Team USA -- defenseman Jake Sanderson -- understands Tkachuk wanting to migrate down south with the Panthers, even if the call Sanderson got from Staios telling him about the trade was hard to hear.

"Looking back, I shouldn't be surprised that Brady wanted to go play with his brother," Sanderson said. "I don't think anybody should be. But to see it actually happen was crazy. He was such a big personality and leader in our room, so things will be different for sure."

Sanderson has been sidelined by an injury early this season but is projected to get back in against Florida. If all goes well, he'll be trying to keep Tkachuk from running wild in his old barn.

"It'll be a high-compete game," Sanderson said. "Obviously with Brady coming back, that's a [big thing]. But you have to separate the two and be like, we're playing the Florida Panthers. That's the most important thing."

Tage Thompson was an emergency recall for Team USA at 4 Nations but a full participant on the Olympics journey, when he saw firsthand a masterclass in brotherly bonding play out.

"Really, what you see is what you get with [Brady] and Matthew," Thompson said. "I feel like they're a wide-open book. Both really big personalities. They rile each other up and bounce off each other. So it's fun to be around. It keeps the room light, and I think you need that, especially during the season.

"It's a long regular season. There's going to be a lot of ups and downs, and anytime you can keep the room light, I think it just kind of helps focus on just a day at a time and not think about the past or way too far about the future. So they do a good job of that."

Brady has the same sort of pesky persona on the ice as Matthew -- Brady's 812 penalty minutes in 576 career games with the Senators is second most in franchise history -- that makes him as terrifying an opponent as he is a terrific teammate. It's a frustrating, fascinating dichotomy that Thompson, having experienced both sides, can appreciate and abhor.

"Brady's always been one of those guys that you absolutely hate playing against but love on your team," Thompson said. "He's a lot of fun to be around, someone that just comes to the rink and he just has fun with the game, and that's what it's all about. It doesn't really matter the circumstance or the stage, it's all about having fun.

"But then at the same time, when it's time to go out there and do your job and compete, he's one of the best at it. That's why I think guys who play with him always love him so much."

It's also another part of what Tkachuk said made parting with the Senators emotionally fraught. Tkachuk had good friends inside and outside the dressing room -- and still does. Ottawa wing Drake Batherson planned to see Tkachuk for dinner the night before Wednesday's game to catch up with a pal he couldn't fault for handling his own business.

"Guys in their careers, they are going to do whatever they are going to do," Batherson said. "It's not going to change the relationship I have with him because [he] wants to play somewhere else. We are still going to be friends."

Tkachuk's departure hurt the Senators' short-term prospects. That alone could have led to some difficult conversations before he closed the door behind him in Ottawa.

"It was a small group of people that knew," Tkachuk said of spreading the news. "I had conversations with a couple guys before. And I made some phone calls after. There's some guys that I spent eight years with. [We] went through a lot of tough times. And I think through those tough times, through the adversity, you just get so close that they're not just teammates -- they're family."

And now, it's time for the prodigal son's return.

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at United States GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli, it's too late

- Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant Singapore drive

- Hamilton calls Singapore strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.
